results.result: Over 200 different SARS-CoV-2 lineages were detected in Mexico during the first year of the epidemic (January 2020 to November 2021), with only five lineages (B.1.1.222, B.1.1.519, B.1.1.7, P.1, and B.1.617.2) displaying dominant prevalence patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C27, and C44 are supported by data analysis of genome sequences from GISAID and citations to published reports. The identification of dominant lineages is confirmed through comparative analysis of temporal distribution patterns shown in Figure 1.

results.result: Lineages B.1.1.222 and B.1.1.519 likely originated in Mexico, each forming single extended transmission chains that persisted for over 16 months. Both lineages dominated in Mexico but never dominated in the USA, despite being seeded back and forth between the two countries.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C34, C59-C60, C64-C65, C77-C79, C83, C173-C174 are well-supported by phylodynamic analyses showing high posterior probabilities (PP: 0.99) for Mexican origin, MRCA dating, and phylogeographic patterns documented in Figures 2a-b. The persistence estimates are based on inferred node dates in MCC trees.

results.result: Lineages B.1.1.7, P.1, and B.1.617.2 were characterized by multiple introduction events into Mexico (224, 130, and 142 events respectively), resulting in a few successful extended local transmission chains that persisted for 10, 5-7, and 7 months respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C35, C91-C93, C107, C117, C138, C184 are supported by phylodynamic analyses quantifying introduction events with 95% HPD intervals and identifying extended transmission chains shown in Figures 3 and 4. The persistence estimates are based on inferred MRCA dates.

results.result: Many clades from different lineages were distributed within the southern region of Mexico (Chiapas, Yucatán, Quintana Roo, Campeche), suggesting this area played a key role in SARS-CoV-2 spread. For B.1.617.2, viral diffusion patterns showed seeding from the south with subsequent movement into central and northern regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C36, C158-C160, C171, C186, C190 are supported by phylogeographic analyses showing clade distributions and well-supported viral transitions (BF >100, PP >0.9) documented in Figure 4 and Table 1. The southern region pattern is consistently observed across multiple lineages.

results.result: The Mexican Consortium for Genomic Surveillance (CoViGen-Mex) was launched in February 2021, aiming to sequence approximately 1200 samples per month. The sequencing output gradually increased from <500 genomes per month to >1000 genomes from May 2021 onwards, contributing to approximately 80,000 total genomes available by the time of writing.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C26 describe the establishment and output of CoViGen-Mex, supported by data from GISAID showing sequencing trends over time. The figures are consistent with stated program goals and documented in the manuscript.

results.result: Despite centralized sequencing in Mexico City, the cumulative viral genomes generated (approximately 100 per 10,000 cases, or ~1% of official COVID-19 cases) correlated with case distribution across states and was sufficient to explore spatial and temporal frequency of viral lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 are supported by data analysis and visualization in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, showing correlation between genome sampling and case distribution. The adequacy assessment is reasonable given the study's successful characterization of transmission chains.

results.result: For most dominant lineages, peaks in genome sampling frequency coincided with epidemiological waves of infection, with specific patterns observed: B.1.1.222 reached 35% in October 2020, B.1.1.519 reached 75% in January 2021, B.1.1.7 and P.1 peaked at 25% during decreased cases, and B.1.617.2 reached >95% in August 2021.
results.evaluation: Claims C45, C52-C53, C72, C75, C88, C114, C132-C133 are supported by temporal analysis of genome sampling frequencies shown in Figure 1b, correlating with epidemiological data. The patterns are well-documented and consistent with cited previous reports.

results.result: Significant sequencing disparities exist between Mexico and the USA, with B.1.1.222 reaching 35% frequency in Mexico versus 3.5% in the USA, and B.1.1.519 reaching 75% in Mexico versus 5% in the USA, despite the USA generating 4-fold more B.1.1.222 genomes overall.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57, C76, C175 are supported by comparative analysis of genome data from both countries. The disparity reflects different epidemiological scenarios and sequencing efforts, though the interpretation is complicated by the fact that the USA has much higher overall sequencing capacity.

results.result: For B.1.1.222, an estimated minimum of 237 introduction events occurred from Mexico into the USA and 106 from the USA into Mexico. For B.1.1.519, an estimated minimum of 391 events occurred from Mexico into the USA and 121 from the USA into Mexico.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63, C81-C82 are supported by phylogeographic analysis with 95% HPD intervals provided. The estimates are based on discrete trait analysis shown in Figures 2a-b, though the authors acknowledge limitations due to sampling biases.

results.result: B.1.1.7 and P.1 reached lower sampling frequencies (up to 25%) in Mexico compared to other countries, with similar patterns observed in other Latin American countries (Brazil, Chile, Peru), suggesting region-specific dynamics that differed substantially from the USA and UK.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90, C177-C178 are supported by data analysis and citations to published research. The regional pattern is documented through GISAID data, though the authors acknowledge limitations in genome representation for some Latin American countries.

results.result: Seven extended transmission chain clades (C1a-C7a) were identified for B.1.1.7, with the largest clades C3a and C7a dating to February 2021 and persisting for 3-4 months. C3a comprised genomes from 22/32 states, while C7a comprised genomes from 20/32 states.
results.evaluation: Claims C95, C102-C106 are supported by phylodynamic analysis results shown in Figure 3a and supplementary figures. The clade identification, geographic distribution, and persistence estimates are well-documented with specific MRCA dates and state-level sampling data.

results.result: Two major P.1+ clades were identified: C1_P1 (dating to March 2021, persisting 7 months, from central Mexico) and C1_P1_17 (dating to October 2020, persisting 5 months based on tip dates, from southern Mexico). P.1 was introduced independently and later than P.1.17, with P.1.17 displaying more successful spread in the southern region.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C127 are supported by phylodynamic analysis shown in Figure 3b and supplementary figures. The geographic and temporal patterns are well-documented, though the authors note considerable under-sampling for P.1.17 based on long branch lengths.

results.result: Six major B.1.617.2+ clades (C1d-C6d) were identified, with at least four synchronous introduction events in April 2021. The largest clades C5d (most genetically diverse and geographically widespread, comprising AY.100, B.1.617.2, and AY.113) and C6d (AY.20, restricted to central Mexico) persisted for 6-7 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C157 are extensively supported by phylodynamic analysis shown in Figure 4. The clade characterization includes detailed sub-lineage composition, geographic distribution across all 32 states, and temporal persistence estimates based on MRCA dating.

results.result: For B.1.617.2 clade C6d, limited viral spread was observed from central states (Mexico City) into other regions, with well-supported transitions from Chiapas into central and northern regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C162 are supported by phylogeographic analysis results shown in Figure 4—video 2 and Table 1, with well-supported transitions (BF >100, PP >0.9) documented between specific states.

results.result: Human mobility data analysis revealed two mobility peaks: February-April 2021 (coinciding with B.1.1.7 and P.1+ introduction/spread and B.1.1.519 contraction) and August-November 2021 (coinciding with B.1.617.2 expansion). Increased movement was observed for Mexico City and several other states, with intensified connectivity from Mexico City to surrounding states.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C169 are supported by analysis of mobile phone-derived mobility data shown in Figure 1c and supplementary figures. The temporal correlation with viral lineage dynamics is documented, though causality is not established.

results.result: For B.1.617.2 clades C5d and C6d, no correlation was observed between viral transitions and mean connectivity (C5d: R²=0.007, p=0.008; C6d: R²=0.32, p<2.2e-16) or pairwise distance between states (C5d: R²=0.011, p=0.045; C6d: R²=0.023, p=0.104).
results.evaluation: Claims C170 and C208 are supported by statistical analysis with specific R-squared values, F-statistics, and p-values provided. However, the interpretation is complex: while C5d shows no correlation, C6d shows a moderate R² of 0.32 with highly significant p-value, which contradicts the claim of 'no correlation.' This appears to be an error in interpretation by the authors.

results.result: Ranking connectivity between the southern region (Yucatán, Quintana Roo, Chiapas, Campeche) and the remaining 28 states revealed consistently high bidirectional movements, particularly with Campeche, Mexico City, and Veracruz.
results.evaluation: Claim C172 is supported by mobility data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2. This finding helps contextualize the phylogeographic patterns observed for multiple lineages in the southern region.

results.result: Differences in B.1.1.7 dynamics could be explained partly by competition between lineages (exemplified by co-circulation of B.1.1.7, P.1, and B.1.1.519 in Mexico). A shared genetic background between B.1.1.519 and B.1.1.7 (mutation P681H) may have limited B.1.1.7 spread. Dominance and replacement patterns were driven by lineage-specific mutations impacting growth rate and competition at local scale.
results.evaluation: Claims C179-C180, C200-C201 represent speculative inferences about lineage competition and the impact of shared mutations. While the observations about co-circulation and mutation patterns are documented, the causal mechanisms proposed lack direct experimental validation. The authors acknowledge that lack of representative genomes prevents testing this hypothesis at larger scale.

results.result: B.1.1.519 displayed two amino acid changes in the Spike protein relative to B.1.1.222: T478K (in RBD, impacting antibody neutralization) and P681H (upstream of furin cleavage site, potentially enhancing entry, reducing antibody recognition, and conferring interferon resistance). These mutations may have contributed to B.1.1.519 dominance, with Rt of 2.9 versus 1.93 for B.1.1.222. These mutations were not exclusive to B.1.1.519, appearing later in other VOCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C192-C199 are supported by citations to published research on mutation characteristics and Rt estimates from Mexico. The functional impacts of mutations are documented in the literature, though the authors appropriately note that experimental validation is needed to confirm fitness impacts. The Rt comparison provides supporting evidence for the hypothesis.

results.result: Lineage-specific replacement and dominance patterns are likely shaped by the immune landscape of the local host population. In Mexico, extended exposure to B.1.1.222 and B.1.1.519 may have increased immunity levels in a relatively naïve population (33.5% seroprevalence by December 2020). Introduction of more divergent lineages (B.1.1.7, P.1, B.1.617.2) likely caused a shift in immune landscape. Vaccination rate above 50% was only reached after December 2021, suggesting immunity during the first year depended mainly on virus pre-exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C202-C206 represent speculative inferences about immune landscape dynamics, supported by seroprevalence and vaccination data citations. However, the causal relationship between immune landscape and lineage replacement is not directly demonstrated. The reasoning is plausible but lacks direct immunological evidence from the study population.

results.result: Fluctuating mobility patterns in Mexico were consistent with decreased cases following infection waves, likely reflecting changes in travel restrictions. Since geographic distances and mobility did not correlate with viral diffusion patterns, spread could be explained by human movement across borders. SARS-CoV-2 spread in Mexico is linked to mobility across the USA (evidenced by B.1.1.222 and B.1.1.519 patterns) and congruent with migration routes from South and Central America.
results.evaluation: Claims C207, C209-C211 are supported by mobility data analysis, phylogeographic patterns, and citations. The lack of correlation between internal mobility and viral diffusion (C170, C208) supports the inference about cross-border movement. However, the specific migration routes from South/Central America are inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: The successful spread of a virus lineage does not seem linked to higher number of introduction events, but rather to the extent and distribution of transmission chains, with size likely reflecting virus transmissibility.
results.evaluation: Claim C183 is supported by the study's phylodynamic results showing that lineages with fewer introduction events (B.1.1.222, B.1.1.519) achieved greater dominance than those with more introduction events (B.1.1.7, P.1, B.1.617.2). This inference is supported by citation to Grenfell et al., 2004 on transmissibility and transmission chain size.

results.result: The study investigated five dominant lineages (B.1.1.222, B.1.1.519, B.1.1.7, P.1, B.1.617.2) using a phylodynamic approach to analyze publicly available SARS-CoV-2 genome data from Mexico in global context. A human migration and phylogenetic-informed subsampling approach was devised to increase robustness of phylogeographic analyses. Results were contrasted with epidemiological and human mobility data.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C33 describe the study design and methodology, which are well-documented in the Methods section and supported by citations. The novel subsampling approach is described in detail and made publicly available, enhancing reproducibility.

results.result: Study limitations include uncertainty in determining source locations for virus introductions due to regional genome sampling biases, uneven sampling across locations, and poor viral genome representation for many Central and South American countries. These biases likely affect viral diffusion reconstructions, rendering them incomplete. However, SARS-CoV-2 genome sampling in Mexico was sufficient to robustly quantify and characterize lineage-specific transmission chains.
results.evaluation: Claims C212-C217 represent appropriate acknowledgment of study limitations, supported by citations to relevant literature on phylogeographic biases. The authors provide balanced assessment of how limitations affect their conclusions while maintaining that main findings are robust. The validation of the subsampling approach (described in Appendix 1) supports the adequacy claim.

results.result: Most B.1.1.7 genomes from Mexico were generated from Chihuahua, representing the earliest B.1.1.7 genomes from the country. However, only a small proportion grouped within extended transmission chain C2a, with the rest in minor clusters or singleton events. Chihuahua generated overall lower proportion of viral genomes throughout 2020-2021. Mexico City reported the highest number of COVID-19 cases and B.1.1.7 cases (2452) during February-September 2021. Neither phylogenetic nor epidemiological data support Chihuahua as an initial sink-source for B.1.1.7.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C101 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 3a), genome sampling data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and official epidemiological data. The authors appropriately conclude that early detection in Chihuahua does not indicate it was a major source, given the limited transmission chains and lower overall case burden compared to Mexico City.

results.result: The pattern of southern region importance in SARS-CoV-2 spread is comparable to what has been observed for arboviral epidemics in Mexico. Common epidemiological patterns between SARS-CoV-2 and arboviruses may have emerged due to dependence of vector populations on human behavior and mobility patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C187-C188 are supported by citations to published research on arboviral epidemics in Mexico. However, the proposed mechanism for common patterns (dependence on human behavior and mobility) is speculative, especially given the fundamental difference in transmission mechanisms (respiratory vs. vector-borne).
